keyVerseText: And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed. Noah: Gr. Noe: that is Rest, or, Comfort
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מַעֲשֶׂה (maʻăseh) derives from the root עָשָׂה (ʻâsâh), which fundamentally means "to do" or "to make." This etymology highlights ma'aseh as an act or deed that involves intentional accomplishment or production. Beyond the simple English gloss of "work" or "deed," the root sense emphasizes both the process of doing and the tangible outcome of that doing, whether it be labor, craftsmanship, or an enterprise.
usageInScripture: Throughout the Hebrew Scriptures, מַעֲשֶׂה occurs 235 times and is most frequently translated as "the work" or simply "work," indicating a broad semantic range that includes deeds, labor, and accomplishments. Its usage spans from concrete actions and occupations to abstract notions of activity and even products such as poems or possessions. This versatility reveals the word's function as a bridge between human effort and its results, underscoring the importance of both the action and its fruit in biblical thought.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, מַעֲשֶׂה invites reflection on the nature of human responsibility and divine purpose. It reminds believers that their actions—whether acts of obedience, labor, or enterprise—are significant in God's eyes and partake in His sovereign design. As deeds can be good or evil, the word calls for discernment and faithfulness in all undertakings. Moreover, understanding מַעֲשֶׂה as both deed and product encourages a holistic view of Christian life, where faith is expressed through tangible works that reflect God's glory and grace.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 5:29 states, "And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed." Here, מַעֲשֶׂה is translated as "work," emphasizing human labor and effort under the curse of the ground. The term enriches the verse by highlighting the reality of human toil as both a burden and a context for divine comfort through Noah, whose name itself means rest or comfort. This connection underscores God's redemptive provision amid human struggle.
